title: Remove leaf levels
label: idb
statement:
Given an imbalanced binary tree:

Print the leaf nodes.

Remove those leaves.

Print the new leaf nodes.

Continue until only the root remains.

Follow-up:

Solve for an N-ary tree.

qa.a: Most operators (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`) are deferred: nothing runs until enumeration. `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Count()`, `First`, `Sum` execute immediately. `OrderBy` is deferred but buffers everything when enumerated.
The whole pipeline runs twice — including any I/O behind the source. Materialise once with `ToList()` if you need it twice.
An enumerator per operator, plus delegate and closure allocations for captured variables. Negligible for setup code, measurable in a per-request hot path.

qa.q: When is an explicit loop better?
qa.a: Hot paths, early exit with complex state, mutating as you go, or when you need to state complexity exactly — R5 hid an O(n log n) sort per call inside one readable line.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Given an imbalanced binary tree:
> 
> Print the leaf nodes.
> 
> Remove those leaves.
> 
> Print the new leaf nodes.
> 
> Continue until only the root remains.
> 
> Follow-up:
> 
> Solve for an N-ary tree.

Peel the tree like an onion. Take all the leaves, then all the nodes that became leaves, and so on, until nothing is left.

A list of lists: the nodes removed in each round, in order. Round 0 is the original leaves.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
The statement says "continue until only the root remains", which implies the root is never removed — but a root with no children *is* a leaf, so the first round would print it.

Both readings produce the same grouping; they differ only in whether the last round is emitted. I include the root as its own final level, because the sequence of levels is the natural output and stopping one short makes the single-node tree return nothing. Say which you chose.

The second, larger question: **does the tree actually have to be mutated?** "Remove those leaves" sounds like it must. It does not, and that is the point of the question.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| The root is emitted as its own final round. | The alternative stops one round early. Same grouping; only the last line differs. A single-node tree is the test that distinguishes them. |
| Order within a round does not matter. | The recursion produces one particular order. If a specific order were required — left-to-right, say — the traversal order would have to be pinned, which the post-order walk happens to give anyway. |
| Values are not unique. | Nothing here depends on uniqueness. If nodes had to be identified rather than valued, the lists would hold nodes instead of ints. |
| The caller does not need the tree afterwards. | If it does, the non-mutating version is not merely faster, it is the only correct one. Ask — this is a cheap clarification with a real consequence. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
The statement describes a procedure, and the procedure is not the answer.

Ask instead: **which round does a given node belong to?** A node leaves in round 0 if it is a leaf. Otherwise it cannot go until all its children have gone, so it leaves one round after its slowest child. That is

`round(node) = 1 + max(round(left), round(right))`, with `round(null) = -1`

and that expression is **exactly the height of the node measured from the bottom**. So the rounds are not something you perform — they are a property every node already has, and one post-order pass computes all of them. Bucket each node by its height as the recursion returns and you have the whole answer in O(n), with the tree untouched.

The distinction that makes this click: **depth is passed down, height is returned up.** A BFS level counter gives you depth from the root, which is why `103 Binary Tree Zigzag` is BFS and this is not. Anything asking about the *last* level, peeling leaves, or weighting by distance from the bottom needs the post-order return value. That is also precisely why `364 Nested List Weight Sum II` is harder than `339`, its top-down sibling — same problem, same fix.

So the answer to "remove those leaves" is: I do not have to. And saying that, rather than doing it, is the whole question.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Follow the statement literally. Walk the tree collecting leaves, then walk it again cutting the links to them, and repeat until empty. *O(n) per round × h rounds = **O(n · h)**, which on the imbalanced tree the statement specifies is O(n²). O(h) space.*

**Why not good enough.** It is correct, and on a balanced tree it is O(n log n), which is fine. The statement says *imbalanced*, and a degenerate chain of 10,000 nodes makes it 100 million operations for something achievable in 10,000. The deeper objection is that it destroys the input, and nothing in the problem requires that — the caller may well want the tree afterwards.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | The root of a binary tree |
| TRANSFORMATION | Each node’s peel round is recognised as its height from the bottom |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `List<List<int>>`, indexed by height. No queue, no visited set, no mutation. |
| ALGORITHM | One post-order recursion returning height; append each node to `levels[height]` |
| OUTPUT | The list of rounds, and an untouched tree |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- `Height(null)` returns -1.
- Recurse into both children first.
- `h = 1 + max(leftHeight, rightHeight)`.
- If `h == levels.Count`, this is the first node seen at that height — append a new list.
- Add the node’s value to `levels[h]`.
- Return `h`.

- The tree is explicitly **imbalanced**, so the number of rounds is the height, which can be n. That makes a per-round pass O(n²) in the worst case.
- Rounds are determined by the tree’s shape, not by the order you process nodes.
- Mutation is optional — and deciding that is the question.
- Recursion depth equals the height, which for a degenerate tree is n.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| `List<List<int>>` indexed by height | Height values arrive in no particular order, but they are dense from 0 upwards, so a list indexed by height is the natural bucket. A dictionary would work and would need sorting at the end. |
| Post-order, specifically | A node’s height depends on its children, so the children must be resolved first. That is the definition of post-order — the traversal is not a choice here, it is forced by the recurrence. |
| `return -1` for null | So a leaf returns 0 and becomes round 0. Returning 0 for null would make every leaf round 1 and every list index off by one. |
| No mutation | The tree is only read. That makes the function safe to call twice, safe to call on a shared tree, and trivially thread-safe for concurrent readers — none of which the literal reading gives you. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**`if (node == null) return -1;`.** The base case that makes the indices line up. A leaf has two null children, so `1 + max(-1, -1) = 0`, and round 0 is index 0. Return 0 for null and every level shifts by one — the classic off-by-one in this problem, and it produces an answer that is wrong in a way that looks structured.

**`if (h == levels.Count) levels.Add(new List<int>());`.** Heights arrive in whatever order the recursion reaches them, but a node of height h can only be reached after a node of height h-1 has been (its own child), so `levels.Count` is never more than one short. That is why a single `if` suffices rather than a while loop or a pre-sized list — and it is worth stating, because it looks like a bug that happens to work.

**Why `PeelLevels` takes the list as a parameter.** The recursion needs to write into shared state and return the height. Passing the accumulator down is the cheapest way; the alternative is returning a tuple of `(height, levels)` and merging, which allocates per node for no benefit.

**`PeelAndMutate` uses `ref TreeNode root`.** The last round removes the root itself, so the caller’s reference has to be nulled. Without `ref` the caller is left holding a node that the function believes it deleted — the kind of API detail that is invisible in a test and obvious in a code review.

**`Strip` returns the replacement node.** Returning `null` for a leaf is what lets the parent do `node.Left = Strip(node.Left, picked)` and cut the link without needing a parent pointer or a special case for "my child was a leaf". It is the standard shape for tree mutation in a functional style and it removes every null check.

**The N-ary version is the same function.** `h = -1; foreach (child) h = max(h, Height(child)); h += 1;` is `1 + max(children)` with an empty-children base case folded in. Nothing else changes — not the bucketing, not the base case, not the complexity. That is the answer to the follow-up, and the fact that it is this small is the point.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PeelLevels` | O(n) | O(n + h) | Each node visited once; output is n values, recursion is h deep |
| `PeelAndMutate` | O(n · h) | O(h) | One full pass per round, h rounds |
| `NaryLeafPeeling.PeelLevels` | O(n) | O(n + h) | Each node and each child link visited once |

**The O(h) recursion depth is the real risk here, not the time.** The statement says *imbalanced*, and a degenerate chain of 100,000 nodes will overflow the default 1 MB stack. The fix is an explicit stack, or a `Thread` created with a larger stack size. Worth raising — the question hands you the word "imbalanced" and it is the only reason it is there.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Null root | Returns an empty list, no exception. |
| Single node | Returns `[[value]]` — the root is its own round. This is the case that distinguishes the two readings of "until only the root remains". |
| A degenerate chain | h = n, so n rounds of one node each. Correct, and the stack-depth risk. |
| A perfect tree | h = log n rounds, with half the nodes in round 0. |
| Duplicate values | Fine; nothing is keyed on value. |
| One-sided nodes | A node with only a left child has height `1 + max(hL, -1)` = `1 + hL`. The null side contributes nothing, which is what the -1 base case buys. |
| N-ary node with no children | The loop does not execute, `h` stays -1 and becomes 0 — a leaf. The base case works without a special case for empty children. |
| 100,000-node chain | Recursion overflows. Needs an iterative post-order walk or a bigger stack. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Solve it for an N-ary tree.**

`h = 1 + max over all children`, with -1 when there are none. The bucketing, the base case and the complexity are all unchanged.

*Trade-off:* None. The whole point is that the generalisation is free, and it is free because the original solution was written against the recurrence rather than against the binary shape. If the original had been the literal remove-and-repeat version, this follow-up would have needed the removal logic rewritten for a child list.

**Does the tree actually have to be mutated?**

No. The rounds are a property of the shape, so one read-only pass computes them. If the caller genuinely wants the tree destroyed, `PeelAndMutate` does it explicitly — but as a separate, clearly-named operation, not as a side effect of a query.

*Trade-off:* O(n) versus O(n·h), and a preserved input versus a destroyed one. There is no case where the mutating version is better *for computing the answer*; it is only better if destruction is itself the goal. Separating the two is the design point.

**The tree has 100,000 nodes in a chain. Your recursion overflows.**

Convert to an iterative post-order traversal with an explicit `Stack`, carrying computed heights in a `Dictionary<TreeNode, int>` or by pushing each node twice with a visited marker. Alternatively, run the recursion on a `Thread` constructed with a larger stack — which is a legitimate and much shorter answer in C#, and worth offering as the pragmatic option.

*Trade-off:* The explicit stack is robust and roughly doubles the code, and it moves the memory from the stack to the heap where it is bounded by available memory rather than by a 1 MB default. The bigger-thread trick is three lines and only moves the cliff. For a library I would write the iterative version; for a one-off I would raise the stack and document why.

**Return the nodes, not the values. And what if you need the parent of each?**

Bucket `TreeNode` references instead of ints — a type change and nothing else. For parents, pass the parent down as a second argument; it costs one parameter and no extra pass, because the recursion already visits every node with its parent on the stack.

*Trade-off:* Holding node references keeps the whole tree alive from the result, which matters if the caller expected the values to be a lightweight snapshot. Worth a sentence about lifetime, not more.

**Why is this not just BFS with levels?**

BFS gives **depth from the root**; this needs **height from the leaves**. In the worked example, node 3 is at depth 1 and nodes 4 and 5 at depth 2, yet all three leave in round 0. No function of depth produces that grouping, because two nodes at different depths can share a round and two nodes at the same depth can be in different ones.

*Trade-off:* It is not a trade, it is a correctness distinction. `103 Binary Tree Zigzag` is on the supplied list and is the BFS version of a level question; doing the two back to back is the fastest way to internalise which is which.
